prompts.prompt: You have to review pull request ${pr} (branch ${branch}) of the ${GITHUB_REPOSITORY} repository thoroughly, utilizing the tools you have. Delegate work to subagents (delegate_task / collect_results) when it helps: fan out file exploration, blast-radius tracing and convention checks to parallel workers and collect their results, instead of reading everything serially yourself. First check the current state of the PR - existing comments and author replies: on a recurring review, where a reply adequately justifies the change (for example why something was removed), accept it and update or resolve that earlier finding instead of reposting it; where it does not, keep the finding and say briefly why. Read the changed files and the context around them, calculate the impact of the change (use the code-review-graph tools for blast radius, callers and affected flows - build/update the graph first if it is not built), and check whether it follows the standards of this project as per your skills - load repo-conventions for the rules and github-commenting for the format. Once you have all of that, collate the findings and post inline comments on the exact lines with suggestions on fixes for the issues found, plus ONE summary comment for the whole review.

Validate the PR state: list all comments now on pull request ${pr}. Verify every comment you posted landed with clean, user-friendly rich formatting - working suggestion blocks, correct file and line anchors, no broken markdown - and fix any that are malformed. If any comment is duplicated (the same finding or summary posted twice), delete the duplicate and keep one. Reply to any author or reviewer comments that need a response. Also validate the pull request's review state itself, not just the comments: an APPROVE verdict must be reflected as an approving review on the PR, and a NEEDS_WORK verdict as a changes-requested review - set or update the review state so it matches the verdict. Finish only when the PR carries one clean, complete review: one summary, one comment per finding, no duplicates, and a review state that matches the verdict.
